unit.title: Prepare and install basic cable trays

summary: This unit teaches you to prepare for and install basic cable trays: the open ladder, perforated, solid-bottom and wire mesh systems that carry many cables through plant rooms, factories, warehouses and ceiling spaces. You will learn to plan the job from the drawings and cable schedule, work safely at height, mark out and fix supports, cut, join and earth the tray, lay and tie the cables, and check, clean up and report on the finished installation.

blocks.p: A **cable tray** is an open support system for cables: a run of tray sections, fittings and supports that the cables are laid on and tied to. It carries far more cables than conduit or trunking can, lets air reach them so they stay cool, and makes adding or changing cables easy. You will find trays in hotel and hospital plant rooms, factories, warehouses, water and sewage pumping stations, data rooms and above office ceilings. This unit is for Level 2 trainees who prepare and install basic tray runs under supervision.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Plan the job
Read the drawings, specification and cable schedule; walk the route; check the maker's load and span tables; list materials, tools and access equipment.
Work safely
Choose and use access equipment correctly, keep the area below clear, wear the right PPE, handle long lengths safely and isolate nearby circuits before drilling.
Choose tray, fittings and supports
Know the tray types and materials and where each is used; name the fittings and supports.
Mark out and fix supports
Mark level and plumb lines, set brackets and hangers at the right spacing, and fix them with the right anchors or clamps.
Cut, join and fit the tray
Cut square, remove burrs, protect cut edges, join with splice plates and fit bends, tees and risers.
Earth the tray
Keep the earth path continuous at every joint, fit bonding jumpers where needed, connect to the main earth and test continuity.
Lay and secure cables
Lay cables to the schedule, neatly and within the fill limits, keep power and data apart, respect bending radii, tie them in and protect them where they leave the tray.
Check, clean up and report
Inspect the finished run, put faults right, clear waste, record changes and report.

head: System
What it is
Best for
rows: Conduit
A closed tube; cables are pulled through
A few circuits, with strong protection
Trunking
A closed channel with a lid; cables are laid in
Several circuits along walls, with outlets on the run
Cable tray
An open support; cables are laid on and tied
Many cables, large power cables and long runs in plant areas, where air flow and easy access matter

ul: Many plant rooms, pumping stations and factories are near the coast. **Salt air** corrodes plain steel quickly, so the tray material and the protection of cut edges matter.
Most buildings have **concrete** walls and ceilings and many have **steel** roof structures, so you will fix supports with anchors into concrete and with clamps onto steel.
Outdoor trays face strong sun, heavy rain and hurricane winds. Covers, UV-resistant ties and secure fixings are part of the design.

The code used in Jamaica is based on the US NEC, which has its own article on cable trays. You will also see trays made to British, European and US standards; follow the maker's instructions for the system you are using.

blocks.note: The tray maker's instructions and load tables are part of the job documents. A tray that is overloaded, under-supported or badly joined can sag, collapse or lose its earth path. Read the instructions for the system on your job.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Type
What it is like
Strengths
Typical use
rows: Ladder tray
Two strong side rails joined by rungs, like a ladder
Very strong; long spans between supports; plenty of air reaches the cables; easy to tie cables to the rungs
Large power cables, for example from a main switchboard to chillers and pumps in a hotel plant room
Perforated tray (ventilated trough)
A flat base with punched holes, and low side flanges
Supports small cables along their whole length; holes let air through and give tie points
Mixed small power and control cables in factories and plant rooms
Solid-bottom tray
A flat base with no holes, often with a cover
Protects cables from dust, dripping liquids and falling objects; covered, it shields them from sun
Dusty or dirty areas, under pipes, and sensitive cables
Wire mesh (basket) tray
Welded steel wire in a grid
Light, easy to cut and shape on site, open for air and for cables to drop out anywhere
Data and small power cables above ceilings and under raised floors
Channel tray and single-rail tray
A narrow channel, or a single central rail with arms
Small and neat
A few cables, or drops to equipment

blocks.p: Small cables can sag between the rungs of a ladder tray, so perforated or wire mesh tray suits them better. Large power cables, which are stiff and heavy, sit well on ladder tray.

ul: Width: common widths range from about 100 mm to 900 mm.
Side rail height (load depth): often about 50 mm to 150 mm.
Lengths: usually 3 m, sometimes 2.4 m or 6 m.
Each size and type has a **safe load for a given span** (distance between supports), given in the maker's load and span tables.

head: Material or finish
What it is
Where it suits
rows: Pre-galvanised steel
Made from steel sheet that was zinc-coated before it was cut and formed; cut edges are bare
Dry indoor areas
Hot-dip galvanised steel (HDG)
Dipped in molten **zinc** after it is made, giving a thick coat that covers every edge
Damp areas and outdoors away from the worst salt spray
Stainless steel (often grade 316)
Steel that does not rust easily
Coastal and chemical areas, food plants
Aluminium
Light and resists corrosion
Outdoors and coastal areas where weight matters
Fibreglass (FRP)
Glass-reinforced plastic; does not conduct or rust
Very corrosive places, such as near the sea or in chemical and sewage plants
Painted or powder-coated steel
Steel with a paint finish
Indoors, where a colour is wanted

blocks.note: Near the sea, plain or pre-galvanised steel rusts quickly in salty air. Choose the material the spec gives: often hot-dip galvanised steel, stainless steel, aluminium or fibreglass. Use matching fixings: stainless bolts on stainless tray, for example. Mixing metals, such as stainless bolts in aluminium without the maker's washers, can cause corrosion where they touch.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Fitting
What it does
rows: Horizontal bend (30°, 45°, 60°, 90°)
Turns the run while it stays on the same level
Horizontal tee
A branch leaves the run at 90°, in a T shape
Horizontal cross
Four runs meet
Vertical bend (riser), inside or outside
Takes the run up or down to a new level
Reducer (straight, left-hand or right-hand)
Joins a wide tray to a narrower one
End plate (end cap)
Closes the open end of a run
Drop-out (waterfall) fitting
Gives cables a smooth, rounded edge where they leave the tray to drop to equipment
Cover
Protects cables from sun, rain, dust and falling objects
Divider (barrier strip)
Separates power cables from data and control cables in one tray
Splice plate (straight)
Joins two lengths end to end, bolted through both side rails
Expansion splice plate
A splice with slotted holes, which lets a long run grow and shrink with heat
Adjustable (hinged) splice
Makes an angle that no standard fitting gives
Hold-down clip
Fixes the tray to its support
Bonding jumper
A short earth conductor across a joint that may not conduct well

head: Support
What it is
Where it is used
rows: Cantilever bracket
An arm fixed to a wall (or post) at **one end only**; the tray rests on it
Runs along walls
Trapeze hanger
Two threaded rods hung from the ceiling, with a cross-bar (usually strut channel) under the tray
Runs hung from a slab or roof structure
Single-rod hanger
One rod with a centre-hung bracket
Light runs such as wire mesh tray
Floor stand or post
A post fixed to the floor with arms
Plant rooms and outdoor pipe racks
Beam clamp
A clamp that grips the flange of a steel beam
Hanging rods or brackets from steel beams **without drilling** them

blocks.p: **Slotted metal strut channel**, often about 41 × 41 mm, is used to make brackets, trapeze cross-bars and frames. It is cut to length on site and fixed with spring nuts, bolts and the maker's fittings.

head: Fixing
Use
rows: Wedge anchor
Heavy loads in solid concrete walls and floors
Sleeve anchor
Concrete and solid block
Drop-in anchor
Set in a concrete ceiling to take threaded rod
Resin (chemical) anchor
Heavy loads, close to edges, or in hollow block with a mesh sleeve
Beam clamp
Steel beams, without drilling

ul: The largest distance between supports comes from the **tray maker's load and span tables**, for the tray size and the weight of cables it will carry. It is not guessed, and it is not taken from the cable drum label.
The heavier the cable load, the **shorter** the span the tray can safely bridge. If more or heavier cables are added to the design, the spacing must be checked again.
Supports too far apart let the tray **sag or bend** under the cables, which strains splices and fixings.

Put a support **close to each fitting** (bends, tees, risers). Fittings are weaker than straight lengths and must not hang unsupported; makers usually show supports near each end of the fitting, and at the middle of large bends.
Where you can, put **splices close to a support**, not in the middle of a span. Many makers say within about a quarter of the span from a support.

sections.title: Planning the job and the materials list

head: Document
What it tells you
rows: Plan (plan view)
The tray route as if you are looking down from above, with widths and fittings
Sections and elevations
Heights of the tray, and how it passes beams, ducts and pipes
Specification
Tray type, material, finish, maker, support spacing and earthing requirements
Cable schedule
Each cable's number, size, type, route and the equipment at each end
Maker's instructions and load tables
Safe spans, splice and fitting details, bolt torque

blocks.p: Walk the route with the drawings and a tape. Check heights against beams, ducts, pipes, sprinkler pipes and light fittings. Note where bends, tees, risers and reducers are needed, and where the tray passes through walls or floors, especially fire-rated ones. Leave enough space above and beside the tray for people to lay cables now and to add or change them later. If the route clashes with something, such as a new water pipe, stop and report it so a new route can be agreed. Never move another trade's work yourself.

A straight wall run is 10.5 m long. The maker's table allows a 1.5 m span for this cable load, with a bracket at each end. Tray comes in 3 m lengths. Each joint uses a pair of splice plates and 8 bolts. Each bracket takes 2 anchors.

head: Item
Working
Quantity
rows: Tray lengths
10.5 ÷ 3 = 3.5, rounded up
4 lengths
Joints
Four lengths in a line have 3 joints
3 joints: 6 splice plates, 24 bolts with nuts and washers
Brackets
10.5 ÷ 1.5 = 7 spaces, plus 1
8 brackets
Anchors
8 brackets × 2
16 anchors
End plates
One at each end
Bonding
As the drawing shows
Jumpers and an earth connection at the board
Allowance
A few spare bolts and anchors
As agreed

blocks.p: Also list the tools and access equipment: rotary hammer and bits, hacksaw or band saw, files, zinc-rich paint, torque wrench and spanners, laser level, spirit level, tape, square, cable rollers, and a mobile tower or platform. Then list the hazards and their controls, and agree the plan with your supervisor.
Drawings give lengths in millimetres: a gap between two beams of 2.4 m is written **2400**. Multiply metres by 1,000 to get millimetres, and divide millimetres by 1,000 to get metres.

sections.title: Working safely: height, handling and isolation

head: Equipment
Use it for
Key rules
rows: Mobile tower scaffold
Most tray work at 2.5 to 5 m: a stable platform with room for tools and tray

Built by a trained person to the maker's instructions; guard rails and toe boards fitted; outriggers where needed; **castors locked** before anyone climbs; climb inside by the built-in ladder; **never move it with anyone or anything on the platform**
Podium steps
Lower work, around 2 to 2.5 m
Gate closed; wheels locked; on firm, level ground
Mobile elevating work platform (scissor lift)
Higher or longer runs
Only trained and authorised operators; harness where the type requires it
Ladder
Short, light tasks only, such as a quick look
Fibreglass; 1 in 4; three points of contact; never for carrying tray or working with both hands for long

blocks.note: Never stand on cable drums, boxes, the top of a stepladder or the tray brackets themselves to reach a tray. Falls from height are among the commonest causes of serious injury on building sites.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Barrier off** the area under the work and put up warning signs, especially over walkways and where forklifts or the public pass.
Keep tools, bolts and off-cuts in a bag, bucket or tray on the platform, not loose on the tray, so they cannot fall.
Wear a hard hat when there is work overhead, and make sure others in the area do too.
A 3 m length of tray is long and awkward. **Two people** carry it, one at each end, knees bent and back straight, watching for people, doorways and light fittings.
Lift lengths up to a tower platform with a partner, or with a rope and a second person on the platform; never climb with a length in one hand.
Get help with cable drums; use a drum stand or jacks and cable rollers to pay cable out.

head: Task
PPE
rows: Handling cut tray, strut and rod
Cut-resistant work gloves (thin plastic, woollen or kitchen gloves give no protection)
Cutting with a hacksaw or saw
Safety glasses
Drilling concrete, especially overhead
Safety glasses or goggles, a dust mask (concrete dust contains fine silica that harms the lungs), ear protection
Overhead work and site work
Hard hat, safety boots

blocks.p: If a bracket or anchor must go near an existing cable in a wall or ceiling, or an old light fitting must be taken down because it is on the tray route, the circuit is **isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead** first: identify the circuit, tell the people who use the area, switch off, lock off with your own lock and keep the key, fit a tag, prove your tester on a proving unit, test between all conductors at the point of work, and prove the tester again. Drilling 'slowly and carefully' beside a live cable is not a control.

sections.title: Marking out and fixing the supports

flow: Take the route and height from the drawing
Check for hidden cables and pipes along the line with a detector
Mark a level line with a laser level or chalk line at the right height
Mark plumb lines for vertical runs and hanger positions
Mark bracket or hanger positions at the spacing from the maker's table
Add supports close to each fitting and each end
Check the marks against the drawing before drilling

ul: Use a **rotary hammer drill** with a masonry bit of the size the anchor maker gives. Drill to the stated depth, square to the surface.
Wear safety glasses, a dust mask and ear protection. Overhead, dust falls straight into your face: goggles are better than glasses.
**Clean the hole**: blow out the dust with a pump and brush it. Dust left in the hole stops the anchor gripping.
Set the anchor as its maker says: a drop-in anchor is driven open with its **setting tool**; a wedge or sleeve anchor is tightened to the stated torque.
Keep anchors the distance the maker gives from edges and from each other.

blocks.p: Fix each bracket square to the wall and level, with every anchor fitted. Check the line of brackets with a laser or string line before the tray goes on: the tray will follow any bracket that is high, low or twisted.

flow: Fix the top of each rod: a drop-in anchor in the slab or a beam clamp on a steel beam
Cut the threaded rod to length; clean up the cut end
Cut the strut cross-bar to length and file off the burrs
Fit the cross-bar on the rods with a nut and washer above and below it
Level the cross-bar by adjusting the nuts
Lock the nuts tight, and check the hangers line up along the run

ul: After cutting threaded rod, file or grind a small chamfer on the end, or run a nut off over the cut, so the thread is clean and nuts start easily. Cutting through a nut fitted beforehand does the same job.
Use a nut **above and below** the cross-bar so it cannot slide up or down.

blocks.p: Steel roof beams are part of the building's structure. Do **not** drill or weld them unless the structural engineer has approved it: holes and heat can weaken a beam. Use **beam clamps** that grip the flange, rated for the load and fitted as the maker says.

sections.title: Cutting, joining and earthing the tray

flow: Measure the gap on site and check it again
Mark the cut with a square so it is straight across
Clamp the tray firmly so it cannot move
Cut with a hacksaw or band saw, wearing glasses and gloves
File off all burrs and sharp edges
Coat galvanised cut edges with zinc-rich paint

ul: Clamping the tray keeps the cut straight and stops the saw jumping out of the cut and injuring you.
On ladder tray, cut where the maker allows, so the length keeps a rung close to its end.
Wire mesh tray is cut with bolt cutters or the maker's cutter, close to a weld so no sharp spike is left.
An angle grinder throws sparks and burns off zinc: use one only when your supervisor allows, with a hot-work permit where the site needs one, and never near flammable materials.
**Burrs** (the sharp, rough edges left by cutting) cut cable sheaths and hands, so file every one away.
A cut edge on galvanised tray has lost its zinc. Paint it with **zinc-rich (cold galvanising) paint**, or it will rust.
Line up the two lengths and fit a splice plate on the outside of each side rail.
Fit the bolts with the **bolt heads inside the tray** and the nuts outside, so smooth round heads face the cables and the nuts cannot snag or cut them.
Fit **every** bolt the splice takes.
Tighten the nuts to the maker's torque with a **torque wrench**. Loose splices let the run sag and spoil the earth path; over-tightened bolts strip or crush.
Fix the tray to each support with hold-down clips, but on long outdoor runs leave the movement the maker allows at expansion splices.

blocks.p: Fit factory fittings with their splice plates, the same way as straight joints, with a support close to each end of the fitting. Use a horizontal bend to turn on the same level, a vertical bend (riser) to change level, a tee for a branch and a reducer where the width changes.

If a cable is damaged and its live conductor touches a metal tray, the whole tray could become live. When the tray is properly earthed, fault current flows along it back to the supply and the fuse or breaker trips quickly. That only works if the earth path is continuous along the whole run and connected to the main earth.

ul: Clean the contact faces of splice plates; fit all the bolts and tighten them to the maker's torque.
Fit a **bonding jumper** across any joint that may not conduct well: **expansion splices**, adjustable (hinged) splices, painted or coated surfaces, and joins between different materials.
Connect the tray to the main earthing terminal or earth bar as the drawing shows.
Whether the tray itself may act as the circuits' earth conductor depends on the code, the tray's marking and the drawing. Many designs also run a separate earth conductor in the tray.

blocks.p: With the tray dead and no circuit connected to it, zero the leads of a **low-resistance ohmmeter** and measure from one end of the run to the other, and to the main earth. The reading should be low, as the test sheet requires. A high reading means a poor joint somewhere: test section by section, put it right and retest. Record the result. Tapping the tray, or looking at it, proves nothing.

ul: The tray is complete, earthed, tested and free of burrs, swarf and off-cuts.
You have the **cable schedule**, and know where each cable goes in the tray.
Cable rollers are set out along straight runs and corner rollers at bends, so the cables are not dragged over rungs and edges.
Lay cables **neatly side by side**, with as few crossings as possible. Do not twist them together or pile them loosely.
Large power cables are usually laid in a **single layer**, spaced as the drawing shows, so they stay cool.
Do not pull cables tight. A cable pulled tight lifts off the rungs at bends and is strained at its ends.
Use a team for long, heavy pulls, with one person calling the moves, so the cable moves smoothly and nobody gets a hand trapped.
Keep **power cables apart from data and control cables**, with a divider or a separate tray, because power cables can cause interference on data and control signals.
Do not exceed the maker's load or the code's fill rules. An overloaded tray can sag, and crowded cables overheat. Cables should not rise above the side rails.

blocks.p: Each cable has a **minimum bending radius**, usually given by its maker as a number times its overall diameter (D). Bending tighter damages the conductors and insulation. Example: a cable 30 mm across with a limit of 8 × D must not be bent tighter than a radius of 8 × 30 = **240 mm**. Choose bends and risers with a large enough radius.

ul: Tie cables to the tray at regular spacing, as the spec or maker gives. On **vertical runs** fix them much more often, with ties or cleats, so their own weight does not pull them down and strain them.
Use **UV-resistant** (usually black) or stainless steel ties outdoors: ordinary clear nylon ties go brittle in the sun and break.
Tie data cables loosely, or use hook-and-loop straps: over-tight ties crush them and harm their performance.
Cut tie tails flush so they do not cut hands.
Fit a **drop-out fitting** or a smooth edge guard where cables leave the tray to drop to equipment, so the tray edge cannot cut them.
Label each cable at both ends, and along the tray where the spec asks, with its number from the schedule.
Where the tray passes through a fire-rated wall or floor, the opening is sealed with **approved fire-stopping** once the cables are in.

head: Check
What good looks like
rows: Against the drawing
Route, height, tray type and size as drawn, or changes agreed and marked
Line and level
Straight and level along the run, checked with a laser or spirit level
Supports
At the spacing on the drawing, near every fitting; every anchor and bolt in place and tight
Joints
All splice bolts fitted, heads inside, torqued; splices near supports; bonding jumpers where needed
Edges
No burrs; galvanised cut edges painted
Cables
Neat, single layer where required, tied in, labelled, segregated, within fill, protected at drop-outs
Earthing
Connected to the main earth; continuity tested and recorded
Fire safety
Fire-stopping done at fire-rated walls and floors
Finish
End plates and covers fitted; nothing left on or in the tray

head: Fault
Why it matters
Put it right
rows: Bracket with a missing anchor
The bracket can tear out under the load
Fit and tighten the missing anchor
Tray sagging between supports
Span too long for the load
Add supports as the maker's table requires
Splice in the middle of a span
The weakest point is at the place of greatest bending
Add a support near it, as the maker allows
Bolts with nuts inside the tray
Nuts and thread ends can cut cables
Turn them so heads are inside
Bare cut edges on galvanised tray
They will rust
Clean and coat with zinc-rich paint
High continuity reading
A fault may not trip the protection
Find the poor joint, fit a jumper or clean and retighten, retest
Metal filings among the cables
Sharp filings work into cable sheaths with vibration and rust onto the tray
Brush or vacuum them out

ul: Collect off-cuts, bolts and metal filings; put metal in the **scrap metal bin** and other waste in the right bins. Leave nothing on the tray or the floor.
Sweep or vacuum drilling dust.
Take down barriers and the tower only when the work above is finished. Return tools and access equipment, and report any damage.
Count and return unused materials.
Mark any change to the route on the drawing, so the customer has a true **as-fitted** record.
Fill in the job report: the work done, the materials used, the continuity results and any problems.
Tell your supervisor that the tray is finished and checked, and point out anything still to be done.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can explain what a cable tray is and when it is used instead of conduit or trunking.
I can describe ladder, perforated, solid-bottom and wire mesh tray and where each is best used.
I can choose a tray material and finish for indoor, outdoor and coastal sites.
I can name the main fittings, supports and fixings and say what each does.
I can find the support spacing in the maker's load and span tables and explain why supports go near fittings.
I can plan a tray job from the drawings and cable schedule and write a materials list.
I can choose and use access equipment safely, protect people below and handle tray lengths safely.
I can isolate a nearby circuit before drilling or removing an old fitting.
I can mark out a level route and fix brackets, trapeze hangers and beam clamps correctly.
I can cut tray square, remove burrs and protect galvanised cut edges.
I can join tray with splice plates, bolt heads inside, tightened to the maker's torque.
I can keep the earth path continuous, fit bonding jumpers where needed and test continuity.
I can lay cables neatly within the fill limits, keep power and data apart, respect bending radii and tie cables correctly.
I can protect cables where they leave the tray and label them.
I can inspect a finished tray, put faults right, clean up and report.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: Spaces + 1
Supports on a straight run with one at each end
About 41 × 41 mm
Common size of slotted strut channel
Millimetres in a metre: 2.4 m = 2400 mm
Number × D
Minimum bending radius: for example 8 × a 30 mm cable = 240 mm
About a quarter of the span
How close to a support many makers want a splice
1 in 4
Leaning ladder: 1 m out for every 4 m up

terms: Beam clamp
A clamp that grips the flange of a steel beam so a support can hang from it without drilling.
Bonding jumper
A short earth conductor fitted across a tray joint that may not conduct well.
Burr
The sharp, rough edge of metal left after cutting.
Cable schedule
A list of each cable's number, size, type, route and end points.
Cantilever bracket
A support arm fixed to a wall at one end only, with the tray resting on it.
Drop-out fitting
A rounded fitting where cables leave the tray, so the edge cannot cut them.
Hot-dip galvanised
Coated with zinc by dipping in molten zinc after it is made.
Ladder tray
Tray with two side rails joined by rungs.
Load and span table
The maker's table of the load a tray can carry for each distance between supports.
Perforated tray
Tray with a flat base punched with holes.
Riser (vertical bend)
A fitting that takes a tray run up or down to a new level.
Splice plate
A plate bolted across two tray lengths to join them.
Strut channel
Slotted metal channel used to make brackets, frames and trapeze cross-bars.
Trapeze hanger
A support made of two threaded rods with a cross-bar under the tray.
Wire mesh (basket) tray
Tray made of welded steel wire in a grid.

c1.title: Ladder tray in a Runaway Bay hotel plant room
c1.text: Trainee Jovan Murray and electrician Mr Hopeton Ricketts are installing 300 mm wide ladder tray on cantilever brackets along the concrete wall of a hotel plant room in Runaway Bay, St Ann. The tray will carry large power cables from the main switchboard to the chillers and pumps. The maker's load and span table, for the cable load first planned, allows 1.5 m between brackets. The run includes a 90° horizontal bend.

c2.title: Basket tray above a Half Way Tree call centre
c2.text: Trainee Renee Facey and electrician Mr Courtney Dunn are installing wire mesh (basket) tray above the suspended ceiling of a call centre in Half Way Tree, St Andrew. The tray will carry bundles of data cables and some small power cables to the desks below. It hangs from the concrete slab on threaded rod set in drop-in anchors. The gap between the ceiling grid and the slab is small.

c3.title: An outdoor tray at a Yallahs pumping station
c3.text: Trainee Kevaughn Lindo and electrician Ms Sharon Ebanks are installing hot-dip galvanised tray along an outdoor pipe rack at a water pumping station near Yallahs, St Thomas, about 30 m from the sea. The straight run is 40 m long and gets full sun for most of the day. The drawing shows expansion splice plates part way along the run, and covers on the tray.

c4.title: Trapeze hangers in a Four Paths warehouse
c4.text: Trainee Shanoya Grizzle and electrician Mr Patrick Blake are hanging perforated tray 4.5 m above the floor of a warehouse in Four Paths, Clarendon. The tray hangs on trapeze hangers made of threaded rod and strut channel, clamped to the steel roof beams. They work from a mobile tower. Forklifts move goods along the aisle below during the day.

c5.title: Final check at a Savanna-la-Mar furniture factory
c5.text: Trainee Rojae Hamilton and electrician Mrs Beverly Pryce are doing the final check of a tray run in a furniture factory in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, before handing it over. During the job the route was moved 600 mm along one wall to clear a new extraction duct. On the check they find a splice joint sitting in the middle of a span, halfway between two brackets, and metal filings from drilling lying in the tray among the cables.

questions.q: The engineer adds two more large cables to the design after the brackets were planned. What should happen to the bracket spacing?
o: Keep 1.5 m, because spacing depends only on the tray width and nothing else
Space the brackets further apart, since the extra weight holds the tray down
Check it in the maker's table; a heavier load may need closer brackets
Keep 1.5 m, but tie the new cables more tightly so the tray does not sag
questions.why: The safe span depends on the load the tray carries. The heavier the cables, the shorter the span the tray can bridge without sagging, so the spacing is checked again in the maker's load and span table.

questions.q: How are the large power cables usually laid on this ladder tray?
o: In one layer, spaced as the drawing shows
Stacked in two or three layers to save space
Twisted together in one bundle along the run
Piled loosely, then tied in at the very ends
questions.why: Large power cables carry big currents and make heat. Laid in a single layer, spaced as designed, they can lose that heat to the air. Stacked or bundled, they run hotter and must be derated.

questions.q: The heavy cables must be pulled along the tray and round the 90° bend. How should this be done?
o: Dragged over the rungs by a team pulling hard
Pulled tight round the inside of the bend rails
Pushed from the drum end with no help at the bend
Over rollers, with corner rollers at the bend
questions.why: Rollers carry the cable clear of the rungs and edges so its sheath is not scraped, and corner rollers keep it to a safe bending radius at the bend. Dragging and pulling tight damage the sheath and strain the cable.

questions.q: The ceiling installer suggests resting the basket tray on top of the ceiling grid to save time. What should Renee say?
o: Yes, as long as the cables are light data cables
No: it needs its own hangers fixed to the slab
Yes, if the grid is tied up with some extra wire
Yes, provided the ceiling tiles are fitted first
questions.why: A suspended ceiling grid is designed to carry ceiling tiles, not cable trays and cables. The tray must be supported from the building structure, here the concrete slab, on its own rods and anchors.

questions.q: How should the drop-in anchors for the threaded rods be put into the slab?
o: Drill any depth, then tap the anchor in until it feels firm and tight
Drill to the right depth, clean the hole, set it with the tool
Drill an oversize hole so the anchor slides in more easily
Glue the anchor into a shallow hole with building adhesive
questions.why: A drop-in anchor only holds if the hole is the size and depth its maker gives, and is cleaned of dust. It is then expanded with its setting tool. An oversize, shallow or dusty hole lets it pull out under load.

questions.q: Renee ties the data cable bundles to the basket tray. How tight should the ties be?
o: As tight as the tie gun will pull them
So tight the bundle cannot move at all
Tight at the ends and loose in between
Snug, without squeezing the cables
questions.why: Over-tight ties crush and deform data cables and harm the signals they carry. Ties should hold the bundle neatly without squeezing it; hook-and-loop straps are often used for data cables.

questions.q: Why should Renee leave space above the tray, between it and the slab, rather than fixing it hard up against the concrete?
o: So cables can be laid and later added or changed
So that rainwater can drain off the top of the tray
So that the drop-in anchors can be checked by eye
So the tray can be painted after the cables are in
questions.why: A tray is only useful if people can reach into it. Space above and beside it lets the cables be laid in, and lets cables be added, removed or traced later without taking the tray down.

questions.q: Kevaughn cuts a length of the hot-dip galvanised tray. What should he do to the cut ends?
o: Leave them, as the zinc spreads over the cut by itself
Paint them with ordinary house paint to match the tray
File off the burrs and coat them with zinc-rich paint
Wrap them in insulating tape to cover the bare metal
questions.why: The cut has removed the zinc, so bare steel is exposed to salty air and will rust. Burrs are filed off first so they cannot cut cables or hands, then the edge is coated with zinc-rich (cold galvanising) paint.

questions.q: Why does the drawing show expansion splice plates on this 40 m run, and what must go across each one?
o: They let the cables stretch in the heat; a cable tie
They make the run stronger in a hurricane; an extra bolt
They let water drain away after rain; a rubber seal
They let the run grow and shrink; a bonding jumper
questions.why: A long steel run in full sun grows and shrinks each day, and an expansion splice lets it slide without buckling. Because its slotted joint may not conduct well, a bonding jumper is fitted across it to keep the earth path continuous.

questions.q: Which cable ties should be used on this outdoor tray?
o: Clear nylon ties from the indoor stores
UV-resistant black or stainless steel ties
Coloured nylon ties to match the cables
Masking tape wound round every cable bundle
questions.why: Strong sunlight breaks down ordinary clear nylon, which goes brittle and snaps. Black UV-resistant ties or stainless steel ties last outdoors.

questions.q: What are the covers on this outdoor tray mainly for?
o: To shade the cables and protect them from damage
To keep the tray from expanding in the afternoon heat
To make the tray strong enough to walk on during repairs
To stop the zinc coating from wearing off the side rails
questions.why: Strong sun heats cables and breaks down their sheaths over the years, and outdoor cables can be hit by falling objects and debris. Covers protect them; they must be fitted securely so wind cannot lift them.

questions.q: A forklift needs to pass, and the tower is in its way. Shanoya is on the platform with her tools. What should happen?
o: The tower is pushed slowly while she holds the guard rail
She sits on the platform while the tower is moved along
She climbs down with her tools, then the tower is moved
The forklift squeezes past as the tower is held steady
questions.why: A mobile tower is never moved with anyone or anything on the platform: it can tip over, especially at 4.5 m. Climb down, take tools and materials off, move it, lock the castors and check it before climbing again.

questions.q: How is each trapeze cross-bar set level?
o: Bend the strut channel by hand until it looks level to the eye
Pack the tray with wooden wedges wherever it sits too low
Turn the nuts on the rods, then lock them above and below
Hang the cross-bar from one nut and let it settle
questions.why: The cross-bar rests on nuts on the threaded rods. Turning those nuts raises or lowers each end until a spirit level shows it is level. A nut and washer above and below then lock it so it cannot move.

questions.q: Shanoya cuts threaded rod to length with a hacksaw. What should she do next, before fitting nuts?
o: Clean up the cut end so the nuts start easily
Heat the cut end so the thread is hardened
Paint the cut end before the nuts are fitted
Hammer the cut end flat so nuts cannot fall off
questions.why: A hacksaw leaves a burr that stops nuts starting and can damage their threads. A small chamfer with a file, or running a nut off over the cut (fitted before cutting), cleans the thread.

questions.q: Why does the specification ask for beam clamps instead of drilling the steel roof beams?
o: Drilled holes would let rainwater run along inside the beams
Holes can weaken the beams, so drilling needs approval
Beam clamps are cheaper than drilling and give a better earth
The forklifts below could be damaged by falling steel swarf
questions.why: Roof beams carry the building's loads. A hole in the wrong place can weaken them, so drilling or welding needs the structural engineer's approval. Rated beam clamps grip the flange without harming the beam.

questions.q: What should be done about the splice joint halfway between two brackets?
o: Leave it, as a splice is stronger than the tray
Wrap the joint in tape to stop it moving
Add more cables there to hold it down
Add a support close to it, as the maker allows
questions.why: The middle of a span bends the most, and a splice there is a weak point. Makers want splices near supports, often within about a quarter of the span, so a support is added close to the joint.

questions.q: What must be done about the 600 mm change of route along the wall?
o: Mark it on the drawing for the as-fitted record
Nothing, since 600 mm is too small to matter
Tell the customer verbally and leave the drawing
Move the tray back to the original route on paper
questions.why: The customer and future electricians rely on the drawings. Every change to the route, even a short one, is marked on the drawing so the as-fitted record shows where the tray really runs.

questions.q: Why must the metal filings be cleared out of the tray before handover?
o: They make the tray too heavy for its brackets
They carry the tray's earth current away
They make the cables look untidy to the client
They can cut into cable sheaths and rust
questions.why: Sharp filings among the cables can work into the sheaths as the cables move with heat and vibration, and they rust and stain the tray. Brush or vacuum them out, and keep drilling dust away from laid cables.

questions.q: A cable is 25 mm across, and its maker gives a minimum bending radius of 8 times its diameter. What is the smallest radius it may be bent to?
o: 25 mm
100 mm
200 mm
320 mm
questions.why: Minimum bending radius = 8 × D = 8 × 25 mm = 200 mm. Bending tighter can damage the conductors and insulation, so bends and risers must have at least this radius.

questions.q: For an indoor tray in a damp area, which finish gives steel the best protection, including at its edges?
o: Pre-galvanised sheet, cut and formed
Hot-dip galvanised after it is made
Plain mild steel with one coat of paint
Bare steel wiped over with light oil
questions.why: Hot-dip galvanising after the tray is made coats every surface and edge with a thick layer of zinc. Pre-galvanised tray is cut from coated sheet, so its cut edges are bare, and paint or oil gives little lasting protection.
